My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a man-made disaster trauma in a 58-year-old forensic analyst, this item is only coherent if there was a significant physical injury. The rest of the selected profile does not support an injury-based presentation: the threat items emphasize environmental danger and vigilance (limited safe places, loud sounds, unfamiliar places), while the other appraisals are about coping failure and loss of capability rather than concrete bodily injury. With no memory or strategy items to anchor a physical-injury narrative, this appraisal stands out as clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with the supplied cognitive formulation because all cross-node edges are inactive, which implies these components should not appear as tightly linked aspects of one maintaining pattern. However, the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items are strongly conceptually connected: perceiving the world as dangerous maps directly onto restricted safety zones and avoidance of unfamiliar places, creating an active Threat–Negative Appraisal linkage that contradicts the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the content clusters into a classic mutually reinforcing danger/coping pattern rather than isolated components. 'World is a dangerous place' coheres directly with hypervigilance to sounds and avoidance of unfamiliar places, while 'Bad Coper' and 'No longer capable' reflect generalized post-trauma self-evaluation likely tied to the same threat response. With no active edges anywhere in the formulation, this degree of integration is inconsistent.

issues.item: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The formulation specifies no active edges, so the selected nodes should function as relatively isolated components rather than implying a tight linked syndrome. Here the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items form a classic connected PTSD pattern: danger-focused hypervigilance/startle and avoidance are closely mirrored by broad beliefs that the world is dangerous and that the self is incapable. This actively implies strong Threat↔Negative Appraisal linkage, which contradicts the fully disconnected formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within Threat, the items are coherent with each other, and within Negative Appraisals the items are also coherent. The problem is cross-node/formulation consistency: the profile presents mutually reinforcing danger sensitivity and negative self/world beliefs despite all edges being inactive.

vignette:
Rafael Mendez, a 58-year-old forensic analyst, had spent most of his adult life believing that careful observation and procedure could make sense of chaos. That assumption was shattered on a weekday afternoon when a man-made disaster struck the municipal records building where he was working. Rafael had been in a lower-floor evidence room when the blast hit, hard enough to send a wave of heat and debris through the corridor and buckle the lights overhead. In the immediate confusion he heard alarms, cracking concrete, and people shouting names from the stairwell while smoke began seeping under the door. He escaped with others through a side exit, but the image that stayed with him was of a workplace he knew intimately turned into a place he could not read or control in a matter of seconds. In the months that followed, what unsettled him most was not only the memory of the explosion itself but the way ordinary spaces suddenly felt unknowable. He began avoiding unfamiliar places whenever he could, telling his wife that if he did not already know the exits, the crowds, and the layout, he could not assess the danger. A new restaurant, a different route to the grocery store, even an unfamiliar parking garage could make him tense up before he stepped inside, as though his body were bracing for another sudden rupture.

At work, the consequences of that changed way of moving through the world became harder to hide. Rafael still came in, but he took the same route, parked in the same spot, and resisted assignments that required him to visit new sites unless there was no one else available. The municipal building had once been a place where his expertise felt reliable; now, when he walked into an unfamiliar evidence storage facility or a temporary office set up after a fire inspection, he felt his attention narrow immediately to the exits, the windows, the noise in the hall. He described being jumpy, easily startled by a printer slamming shut or a coworker appearing at his elbow. His body, he said, never fully settled anymore. Even at home in the quiet of the evening, he noticed a constant tension through his shoulders and jaw, as if some part of him remained on duty for danger that might arrive without warning. This left him exhausted and irritated, and it fed his growing conviction that his reactions since the disaster showed he was a lousy coper. He had built an identity around being the man who stayed calm when others panicked, the one who could sort evidence, follow the facts, and remain steady under pressure. Now he felt that those traits belonged to someone he used to be. He was no longer sure he could do the things that had defined him for decades, and that loss struck him as humiliating as well as frightening.

Rafael's view of the world had become darker in the same period. He had come to believe that the world is a dangerous place, and he found himself thinking that danger could appear anywhere people gathered, especially in unfamiliar settings where he could not quickly judge what might go wrong. That belief made him even more determined to keep to predictable routines, which narrowed his life in ways his wife noticed before he admitted them himself. He stopped joining her when she wanted to try new neighborhood places and declined an invitation from relatives to meet at a restaurant across town. The avoidance brought short-term relief, but it also left him feeling increasingly cut off from ordinary life and from the part of himself that used to move through the city with confidence. When he had to cross an unfamiliar lobby or enter a new office building for work, he found himself scanning every corner, as if vigilance alone might prevent another disaster. Over time, the strain showed in his posture and in the way he hesitated before agreeing to simple changes in routine.

What finally brought Rafael to seek help was the recognition that the narrowing of his life was no longer something he could explain away as caution. He had been awakened the previous week by a sudden clang from a neighbor's remodeling work and found himself sitting upright, heart racing, unable to settle for nearly an hour. His wife told him he was becoming unreachable, always on edge, always checking, always saying no. Rafael came to treatment not because he believed the disaster was over, but because he feared he was being transformed by it into someone permanently guarded and diminished. More than anything, he wanted to recover a sense that he could move through the world without feeling constantly threatened, and he feared that if nothing changed, the man he once was would remain out of reach.
